parts.text: But how did this ancestral language come to be spoken so widely across Eurasia? During the 19th and 20th centuries, a wide variety of theories were developed about its

. One of these placed its homeland on the vast grassy steppes north of the Black and Caspian Seas around 5,000 years ago.

Subsequent migrations by the pastoral nomads of the Yamnaya culture are thought to have

the ancestral language across Europe and Asia.

The occurrence of such a migration, inferred from archaeology, was debated for over a century with the answer seemingly lost to time. However, thanks to ancient DNA, we now know that large groups of people

from the Eastern European steppes to Europe around 5,000 years ago, providing compelling support for the spread of Indo-European languages from that region.

Today, the spread of Indo-European languages from the steppes is accepted by most

linguists. Yet several questions remain: how did the individual Indo-European languages subsequently spread to their historically known locations?

As part of an international

, led by researchers from the University of Copenhagen in Denmark and Leiden University in the Netherlands, we analysed the DNA of thousands of prehistoric Europeans, including more than 700 newly sequenced individuals. This allowed us to test, for the first time, specific theories on the prehistoric

of the Germanic and Celtic languages.

The first Germanic speakers in Northern Europe?

It has long been assumed that the earliest form of Germanic arrived in Scandinavia with the first steppe

around 4,800 years ago. This event would then have been followed by several millennia of linguistic and genetic continuity.

Our analyses yielded a surprisingly different result. Around 4,000 years ago, a second group with steppe

appeared in Eastern Scandinavia, probably arriving from across the Baltic Sea.

This previously unknown population spread across much of Scandinavia, ultimately matching the region where the ancestral form of Germanic is believed to have been spoken during the first millennium BC.

This

, combined with their ancestry persisting in most later Germanic-speaking populations, suggests these newcomers may have introduced the precursor of the Germanic languages, some 800 years later than traditionally assumed. In this

, the timeline for the language history of Northern Europe is reset.

Anglo-Saxons and Vikings share a surprising past

reading.title: 主旨、理解与信息定位
reading.instruction: 阅读原文后回答 5 道选择题：1 道主旨、1 道内容理解、1 道段落细节、2 道信息定位。段落细节题以题干指定段落为准。

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises the overall focus of this article?
options: Aboriginal astronomical knowledge explains celestial movements and their connections to life on Earth.
A compass works by aligning a magnetised needle with Earth's magnetic field.
Ancient DNA offers new evidence about the origins and spread of Germanic and Celtic languages.
An unusual pair of stars helps explain a repeating radio signal from a dead star.
questions.explanation: 把标题与全文各段的中心内容连起来判断主旨，避免把同一主题下的其他话题当成本文重点。
questions.evidence: At this point, writing spread to northern Europe in the form of the runic alphabet, allowing us to compare migrations with the spread of the Germanic languages we still know today.

questions.prompt: What role is attributed to migrations by Yamnaya pastoral nomads?
options: Preventing every form of language change
Restricting language movement to one modern city
Helping spread an ancestral language across Europe and Asia

questions.evidence: Subsequent migrations by the pastoral nomads of the Yamnaya culture are thought to have spread the ancestral language across Europe and Asia.
